This paper introduces the WeatherCategorization dataset, an annotated collection of 449,043 image instances, each accompanied by textual descriptions, to facilitate effective classification in a multi-class scenario. Due to the variability of weather conditions, both visually and descriptively, this dataset poses a significant challenge for machine learning models. To overcome these difficulties and achieve accurate multi-class classification, this paper presents an ensemble method, incorporating data augmentation from multiple perspectives, along with a novel weight adjustment technique for optimal results. Comprehensive evaluations were conducted using various convolutional neural network architectures, comparing the performance of individual models and our proposed ensemble approach, highlighting their applicability in both image and text modalities. Notably, this paper establishes state-of-the-art performance on the MSRA dataset, reducing error rates by 10% across certain models, and also explores a previously uninvestigated path for improving classification accuracy, ultimately yielding a 5% error rate reduction.

This study aims to deepen the understanding of how climate change is perceived across various global regions and how their perceptions evolve over time. We have gathered unique data from expert interviews with leading scientists in different countries to learn more about how climate change is discussed within each nation's scientific community. These data have been integrated with existing survey results from the Pew Research Center, providing a comprehensive insight into how climate change is viewed across the world by both scientific and general populations. Moreover, we have developed a complex model to analyze the dynamic interplay between these different standards. To the best of our knowledge, this research offers novel contributions in the areas of'science push' and 'institutional push' theories, as well as providing novel empirical evidence.

We introduce an innovative approach to simulate the motion of flexible fingered robotic grippers using the Koopman operator theory. This approach enables efficient regulation of the gripper's fingers to achieve desirable object grasping positions, with improved accuracy over traditional methods. The efficiency of this approach is particularly beneficial for realistic simulations of robotic manipulation tasks, as it significantly reduces the computational demands associated with modeling complex soft robotic devices. The efficacy of this novel strategy has been successfully demonstrated in both virtual reconstructions and real-world experiments involving the manipulation of various objects.

Researchers discovered that certain algorithms like gradient descent, when operating on specific matrices, never produce zero entries. They extended this finding by showing that a similar phenomenon occurs with algorithms based on the minimization of square matrix divisions. These discoveries were made through the analysis of matrix division minimization problems, which were initially framed as free abelian semigroup validation problems. Researchers then applied results from dynamic topological invariant theory to establish criteria for the impossibility of zero entries in matrix division minimization problems, especially those involving organic matrices. These findings were further connected to the generalization of gradient descent algorithms.

A double-peaked broad emission line has been found in the spectrum of a z = 4.575 quasar, which has also been discovered in multiple radio observations. There is a faint, point-like radio source with an estimated flux density of 0.6 $\mu$Jy at 3 GHz that has been localized to less than 12 parsears from the quasar's known location, as determined by recent radio maps. Additionally, a pair of discrete, oriented arcs in the diffraction pattern of historical VLA data at 20 GHz have been identified as likely produced by the quasar's emission. Given the likelihood that the quasar is in an early stage of its evolution, it is proposed that the broad emission line be confirmed as a P~14 day periodicity and monitored for future changes.

Lung cancer patients who are smoke-free are more likely to survive for five years or longer compared to those with a smoking history. To improve survival rates, accurate tumor prognosis is crucial in determining the most effective treatment for each individual. Current lung cancer prognostic systems are limited by their reliance on smoking status data, making them inadequate for patients who do not use tobacco products. To overcome this shortcoming, researchers have created a non-smoking-focused prognostic system, which will be discussed in this paper. To establish a more comprehensive lung cancer prediction model, experts combined clinical data with medical imaging, incorporating machine learning and deep learning techniques to analyze the combined information. The proposed system was tested using data from the Medical University of Vienna's Center for Experimental Molecular Medicine and evaluated its reliability through simulation studies, highlighting its advantages over existing prognostic models that take smoking habits into consideration.

A well-defined language state in reinforcement learning encompasses all relevant linguistic elements, encompassing syntax, semantics, and pragmatics. Traditional reinforcement learning techniques frequently disregard the complexity of genuine languages, instead utilizing artificial languages or simplified versions of them. There have been recent breakthroughs in employing genuine languages, which we will discuss in this review, along with their underlying structures and the computational methods utilized for representation and encoding. The article delves into the purposes of linguistic descriptions within reinforcement learning, presents an analysis of the progress made so far, and identifies areas for further investigation.

A novel approach combining machine learning with mathematical modeling is introduced, enabling the reconstruction of a distribution function from a set of observed spectral features in a redshift of $z>2$ and a temperature of $kT>4$ keV using quasar spectra. Traditional methods rely on the average emission profiles, but are susceptible to biases at high temperatures and redshifts, and are also limited by requiring prior knowledge of the distribution function, which may not always be the case. In contrast, this proposed method utilizes a supervised learning technique with a universal neural network, trained using a large dataset consisting of 472 unique temperature and redshift combinations. Employing this model, an estimated distribution function can be obtained without relying on prior assumptions, and by utilizing the Fackerbarth-Hamann quasar spectrum dataset, the method is validated with promising results, and further refinement is anticipated to yield even more accurate outcomes.

This article examines the Lie algebras of derivative operators, $\frak d_4$, $\frak d_5$ and $\frak d_{2n}$, and their homologous Lie algebras, $\frak g_4$, $\frak g_5$ and $\frak g_{2n}$. The articles identifies the vacuum modules of these Lie algebras under the action of the element $U(\frak h)$, determines the dimensions of the modules, and calculates the central elements of the Lie algebras, $\frak g_4$, $\frak g_5$ and $\frak g_{2n}$.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent breakthroughs in large language models have enabled the construction of comprehensive knowledge bases and have significantly improved the accuracy of open-domain conversation systems. However, the task of open-domain conversation remains an unsolved problem, as existing models often produce irrelevant, repetitive, and formulaic responses. This study presents a novel approach to open-domain conversation that incorporates sophisticated control mechanisms to facilitate more effective and engaging conversations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by creating a role-defined open-domain conversation system, which consistently receives positive feedback from human evaluators. The system's superiority is showcased through comprehensive evaluation of its performance compared to a conventional open-domain conversation model.

The explosion of gravitational wave measurements from compact binary mergers has opened doors to observing the cosmos in new ways, including the possibility of detecting the backdroph of gravitational waves that persist across multiple events in a network of observatories. This "memory" of gravitational waves is caused by the acceleration of masses and can be used to investigate the acceleration of particles in new dimensions. Current theories predict that this gravitational wave background will be overwhelmingly dominated by the oscillations of supermassive black holes, and the amplitude of this background will be out of reach for current and future gravitational wave detectors. However, the volume of gravitational waves that carry the gravitational wave memory is significantly greater than previously thought, and the gravitational wave background detected so far is likely to be caused by the volume of all galaxies in the universe rather than the oscillations of supermassive black holes. This new understanding opens the door for a new area of research, and the gravitational wave community can take advantage of the advancements in gravitational wave detection capabilities to gain a deeper insight into the acceleration of particles in new dimensions.

A hypothetical state of matter, known as the "quasi-degenerate vacuum state," contains an infinite number of nearly equivalent states that can persist for an indefinitely long duration of time. If this state of matter were to exist, it would likely result in extremely massive particles produced at cosmological events, including the creation of black holes and cosmic gravitational waves. To study the effects of this state of matter, researchers developed a mathematical model based on supersymmetry and its breakdown, and found that it can explain the observed amounts of dark matter and normal matter in the universe. Additionally, this model predicts the existence of extremely massive particles, called "leptons," which can potentially lead to an asymmetry in particle matter, and the possible creation of extremely massive black holes with masses similar to those of red dwarf stars.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented by incorporating artificial intelligence elements into the semantically enhanced signaling mechanism. To facilitate emergent semantic communication, a unified framework is designed, combining neuro-symbolic reasoning with causal inference to describe the strategic interaction between senders and receivers in the context of targeted data transmission. Based on this description, a novel game-theoretic model is developed, which reveals that the equilibrium solution yields maximum information gain for both parties. Furthermore, this model is experimentally verified in a hardware setup, demonstrating that the proposed controller based on the predicted Nash equilibrium can successfully manage the communication system and showcase the system's key properties, including reduced data overhead and enhanced information efficiency.

In recent years, various machine learning techniques have been successfully applied to text-based data analysis, with a particular focus on term-level analytics. A key challenge in this domain is term-level classification, which becomes even more complex when working with rare terms that lack sufficient context. To address this issue, researchers have made significant contributions, including the development of Advanced Naive Bayes, an accurate and efficient modeling tool for term-level data. Building upon this work, we introduce a new system, the Hybrid Framework for Term Prediction, which combines Advanced Naive Bayes with an existing term prediction framework, integrating their capabilities to effectively handle rare terms and provide valuable insights into latent concepts. To showcase its effectiveness, we apply the Hybrid Framework to two real-world applications, successfully achieving notable results in enhancing existing models' performance and opening up new possibilities for text-based analysis and interpretation.

Recent sessions-based recommendation models have gained popularity due to their capacity to incorporate sequential user behavior in real-time. These models typically learn to predict the next action (e.g., item selection) (NADAR, 2018) or the ranking of candidate items for the next interaction (e.g., GNNRec, 2019). (Rendle et al., 2010) introduced the concept of listwise ranking to address the inherent order of recommendations. To address the issue of the "same item appearing multiple times in the recommendation list" in two-phase session-based models, this paper proposes a new listwise ranking representation. To overcome this limitation, this paper offers a novel solution by utilizing the fact that the ranking of candidate items can be expressed as a result of multiple selection events. To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces a new two-phase session-based recommendation model, the Inverted Multi-Step (IMS) model, which represents the ranking of candidate items as a result of a series of unidirectional selections. To address the issue of exposure of the same item in the recommendation list, this paper develops a simplified approach by combining the selections into a single process with an inherent order. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the IMS model outperforms state-of-the-art session-based recommendation models, while the inverted representation of the model's internal steps is found to be equivalent to the GNNRec model.

In recent years, researchers have created highly active soft matter systems such as active polymers and swarming colloidal particles to study unique phenomena and potential applications. While it's become feasible to design these systems with diverse forms of activity, such as oscillating optical properties, it remains challenging to control their behavior when confronted with varying levels of activity. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a general method to create dynamic gradients of activity in colloidal systems using laser light. This technique allows us to manipulate the response of individual particles to activity changes and observe significant effects on their behavior, such as enhanced movement and altered response to external stimuli. Additionally, we've identified distinctive features in the particles' movement patterns, including irregular motion and collective behavior, that could serve as indicative signs in active matter systems.

This research project delves into developing and applying advanced numerical methods to simulate the interaction between fluids and solids in three-dimensional fracture networks. Both the fracture spaces and the surrounding matrix are treated as complex geometric environments that require precise meshing for the sake of computational accuracy. We employ a novel meshing technique called GPsMesh, which utilizes a probabilistic approach to generate consistent and conforming grids throughout the matrix and fracture spaces. We combine this meshing capability with two distinct numerical strategies: a traditional finite element method adapted for discrete fracture networks and a more innovative mimetic finite element method, originally designed with stability in mind. The latter approach offers a formidable alternative, albeit initially, lacking direct comparison with other methods in the literature. In the case of single-phase flow scenarios, our findings show the mimetic method to be robust and efficient in the fracture domain, while the modified Taylor-Garrett model outperforms the comparative finite element method in the matrix region. Nonetheless, concerns arise when dealing with multi-phase scenarios, where spurious states threaten the accuracy of our simulations, highlighting the necessity for further model assessment.

This study introduces an innovative approach for a swarm of drones to maintain a formation around moving objects in various shapes and sizes. Drones in the swarm autonomously select leaders that prioritize staying near the center of mass (CM) of the swarm and the object of interest. To prevent collisions, each drone tracks the CM and uses it as a reference point to calculate its optimal trajectory. The swarm's behavior is likened to a registration process in computer science, where points in 3D space are aligned based on the CM, demonstrating cellular structure preservation. The outcome is a swift and collision-free movement of the drone swarm that stabilizes around the CM of both the swarm and the object.

The Seidel matrix of a graph $G$ is defined as the matrix $M_G$ where the entry $m_{ij}$ is $1$ if vertices $i$ and $j$ are connected, and $0$ otherwise. We investigate the Seidel matrix of chain graphs, a subclass of bipartite graphs, and find the possible spectral values, energy, and eigenpolynomials.

This research investigates a mean-field optimal control issue involving stochastic differential equations with delays, driven by fractional Brownian motion, and subject to linear constraints and bounded control functions. It is established that the existence of a unique mean-field optimal control, satisfying these conditions, by demonstrating the relationship between the fractional Brownian motion and its conditional density, applying the diagonalization method, and leveraging the properties of fractional Brownian motion.

For the Dirac operator on $\mathbb{R}^2$ with a twisted convention, 
we model its non-self-adjoint nature by incorporating a first-order 
skew-self-adjoint operator, $\im\J$. We then establish the existence and 
locates (to second order) in a twisted $m$-version of the Weyl formula for 
finite-band energies of the resulting operator $\D_\twisted = i\J + \D$. 
Notably, these results are fully robust against band-crossing phenomena.

The increasing complexity of vehicular networks is addressed by introducing a two-tier architecture, incorporating Roadside Units and Vehicle Relays to enhance communication coverage and reliability. Our proposed framework utilizes a Tier-1 relay as a floating anchor, establishing connections with both vehicles and RSUs within its coverage area. A notable feature of this setup is the use of the vehicle as a relay, effectively addressing blind spots and improving network performance. Our implementation demonstrates the efficacy of this two-tier approach, showcasing that Vehicle Relays can indeed boost the communication capabilities of vehicular networks, thereby rendering them more suitable for life-critical applications.

Wikipedia's vast knowledge is comprised of over 50 million articles, yet their quality is inherently inconsistent.  This project aims to utilize Wikipedia's metadata to identify and categorize articles based on their content, rather than relying on the existing quality tags.  Our research focuses on one such aspect - articles that require extra attention due to their geographic bias.  By analyzing editing patterns and connections within the neighborhood of each article, our model successfully identifies and differentiates biased articles from those that are well-balanced, with an impressive 0.85 accuracy.  Furthermore, our approach demonstrates compatibility with existing Wikipedia metadata, enabling the extension to classify articles according to various other types of incomplete information.

One of the primary issues with adapting advanced software testing techniques to real-world applications lies in the significant expertise required to implement them. This issue can be attributed to various factors such as the reliance of these techniques on specific assumptions, the absence of transparent decision-making mechanisms and the inability to evaluate their results without extensive domain knowledge. In this paper, we address the challenge of making these techniques accessible and efficient for users without in-depth technical knowledge by introducing a novel framework. This framework leverages the user's understanding of their system under investigation to facilitate effective evaluation of testing techniques without necessitating in-depth domain knowledge. In doing so, it bridges the gap between advanced software testing techniques and the users who can significantly benefit from them, thereby making these techniques more accessible and efficient in real-world settings. This paper also highlights an interesting connection between decision-based black-box and zero-shot learning frameworks, enabling the transfer of testing techniques from one domain to another in an entirely data-free environment.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

We've developed a method to express standard geometric T-duality in a bundle form, applicable to a variety of tori modifications. Our technique is particularly useful in identifying concrete realizations of geometric T-duality on principal tori G-doubled bundles and tori double-folded over G. Furthermore, we demonstrate that geometric T-duality can be applied to a wide range of torus configurations by combining our bundle formulation with the G-doubling and double-folding transformations.

In recent years, autonomous systems have become increasingly skilled at gathering data, yet analyzing this information proves to be a significant challenge. The expense associated with training these autonomous entities often poses a substantial barrier. To address this issue, expert input can be utilized to identify the most relevant data - in terms of labeling errors and educational value - during the training process. Rather than having experts constantly oversee operations, we have developed an innovative approach that leverages data collected through cooperative observations between autonomous entities and experts. The system can then learn to pinpoint significant data points, called milestones, which require expert attention, based on past collaborative experiences, thus eliminating the need for constant expert supervision. Threshold-based milestone detection and editing mechanisms are also implemented to ensure that the most critical data points are consistently marked, even when experts are unavailable. Subsequently, we have conducted various tests using this system on diverse datasets, demonstrating its ability to provide reliable milestones, reduce redundant data, and accelerate training times.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal solution on a Hamming grid, leading to a precise computation of the minimum and maximum distances between a set of grid points. These results are particularly beneficial for determining the parameters of a PAC code, given a code rate, ccode size, and maximum code density. To validate our approach, the code parameters of a $[64, 9, 28]$ PAC code are calculated through an example.

A novel approach to tracking the movement and shape of human hands in unstructured point cloud sequences is introduced, usable in the absence of RGB data without ground truth. Our method, tailored for outdoor scenarios devoid of a stable background, relies on the analysis of individual hand features, and does not require the ground truth. Instead, it utilizes information derived from the continuous interaction of hands with environment-based objects. This approach can detect the orientation and movement of hands with the aid of a dynamic template, and then uses a tracking-by-reconstruction technique that incorporates a variational autoencoder to piece together the sequence of the hand's movements. Performance is optimized by regularly updating the reconstructed shape of the hand and incorporating the spatial relationships of the features. This approach shows significant advancements over existing solutions in challenging outdoor scenarios.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of order 40, resulting in a generalized group of order 40 with a noncrystallographic tail-triangle diagram of grade 4, featuring an interlacing number of 2.

A versatile approach to robot operation involves utilizing a depth camera for precise calibration, a task made complex by the depth camera's inherent inaccuracy and the need to account for varied environments and equipment. The depth camera's calibration in a laboratory setting does not guarantee accurate measurements in a different environment, a problem known as the "out-of-vocabulary" challenge. The authors have developed an innovative machine learning-based solution to overcome this issue by training a robot using a diverse range of objects and settings to map pixel patterns to physical measurements without the need for initial calibration. The researchers tested this method using a suction end-effector and a depth camera on a JACO2 robot arm, achieving accurate results in two unfamiliar environments. The results demonstrate the potential for this approach to efficiently calculate end-effector positions and execute tasks in a wide range of settings.

This paper examines the problem of detecting treatment interference in the context of the k-nearest-neighbors (KNN) interference model. Under this model, an entity's outcome is influenced not only by their treatment but also by the treatments received by up to k other entities. From a given set of n treatment combinations, we aim to determine the natural course (control) versus the treated outcomes for every treatment regime from a set of T options, all within a fixed conditional dependence structure known as the 'identifiable counterfactual framework'. However, in the context of the KNN interference framework, this task is characterized by an explosive number of potential interferences, which complicates the process of identifying treatment interference. One notable challenge arises from the fact that any given treatment can be likened to a 'condom package' - the protected or unprotected nature of the treated individual significantly impacts the outcomes of the surrounding entities. Our approach involves formulating the problem of identifying treatment interference under the KNN framework as a novel statistical testing paradigm that needs to differentiate between two distinct joint distributions: the distribution of the actions and their interactions in the treated versus the control group. Our results under specific conditions, particularly when the number of treatment options k approaches infinity, reveal that the null hypothesis of no interference can be rejected with confidence as the number of samples approaches infinity. Conversely, when the number of samples approaches infinity under the null hypothesis of no interference, the test's power also increases indefinitely. Unfortunately, our results yield a

The possibility of Dark Matter consisting of a pseudoscalar particle is explored, 
and the consequences of its interaction with neutrons, protons, and gamma rays 
in Neutron Star collisions and the resulting bright radiation are considered.
This involves calculating the luminosity and energy production throughout the star,
as well as the impact on the star's cooling age and surface brightness.
The study takes into account the composition of the star consisting of neutrons, protons, and electrons,
and the reaction rates within its core.
The analysis reveals that the Dark Matter-induced energy production within the star's core
can affect its cooling age and surface brightness, thus offering the possibility of
interpreting evidence of Neutron Star Dark Matter interactions.
This investigation specifically focuses on the specific case where the Dark Matter particle
has a mass less than the nucleon mass and the reaction involves three-body collisions.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, covering 1,600 deg$^2$ with 21.9 mag depth. ShapePipe is an advanced pipeline designed for accurate galaxy shape measurement, utilizing the Ngmix algorithm and incorporating robust calibration methods and 2D image denoising. Unlike other pipelines, ShapePipe's calibration system is specifically tailored to maintain optimal performance for a given galaxy selection, rather than being limited by depth biases. Furthermore, the pipeline incorporates a denoising step before calibrations, reducing the influence of noise on the measurement of galaxy shapes. Ultimately, ShapePipe demonstrates superior shape calibration results compared to the established Pipe3D pipeline on UNIONS/CFIS data, with an exceptional 0.85 arcsec effective radius uncertainty at 21.9 mag depth. Utilizing ShapePipe, we conducted a comprehensive weak-lensing study of the UNIONS/CFIS dataset, mapping the large-scale structure and employing a machine learning approach to detect the most prominent shear signal, which we found to closely align with the cosmic structure at 20-25 mag depth.

This broad survey of diophantine approximation encompasses several newly emerged as well as crucial results across various fields of study, including transcendental number theory, the study of almost periodic functions, ergodic theory, thin sets, and the distribution of continuous functions on the circle $S$ and the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$. Many significant findings detailed herein stem from our prior works listed in the referenced bibliography. Furthermore, several proven outcomes presented here serve as special cases of, and offer alternatives to, the multiple conjectures proposed within those publications. Notably, we introduce two novel conjectures, one related to the distribution of functions within the countable set $C[S]$ and another concerning the density of sets $E_\beta$ within the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.

We establish that for k-rational and k-Du Bois local complete interplays, the k-rational local complete interplays are k-Du Bois, and the k-Du Bois local complete interplays have a natural k-Du Bois structure.

We utilize a 2D Heisenberg model simulated with around 4,000 spins paired with a pair of helical magnetic markings etched into a ceramic material to investigate the interplay between temperature and spin correlations. At moderate temperatures, the correlations associated with the markings adhere to a predicted model, but it's also discovered that the correlations can be dynamically manipulated by adjusting the characteristics of the markings. This unique property could potentially be utilized to advance the development of materials that respond to changes in temperature or spin.

In the absence of an ultra-high-energy collider, we explore a novel idea at the intersection of quantum gravity, axion-like particles, and neutrino dark matter. Within the multidimensional framework, these axion-like particles can exist as moduli, facilitating the creation of an invisible, gravitationally-attracted substance that permeates space-time and is detectable through its impact on the cosmic microwave background. This axion-like substance, comprising sterile neutrinos, is characterized by its own temperature and chemical potential, differing from the CMB temperature and chemical potential, and is thus detectable via CMB anisotropy patterns. This distinctive concept is contrasted with the concept of a perfect fluid, highlighting its distinct predictions. This theory is further refined by estimating the minimum mass of the sterile neutrinos, demonstrating that their mass is below the GeV level. This framework is scrutinized against various constraints, including the Karlsruhe Tritium Decay data, SNO data, and CMB measurements, and found to be unaffected. This analysis is accompanied by a mathematical formulation of the low-energy quantum gravity in the Kangarajua-Duvvi-Venugopal N=1 supersymmetric theory.

Quantum error correction using the fault-tolerant approach employed in topological codes, particularly those classically simulable, has sparked interest in developing new techniques that can tolerate faults without relying on non-classical states. The use of magic states in such protocols has led to the development of upper limits on the stabilizer rank in various scenarios. This research aims to refine those limits using established mathematical theories, involving the conversion of magic states into stabilizer forms through the use of unitary transformations. The study presents improved upper limits on the stabilizer rank for both universal and restricted Clifford classes, leveraging the concept of charge to achieve these results. The enhancement of these limits is notable, particularly in the case of restricted Clifford, where the limit is improved by a factor of $\chi_{\Phi}^2$ over a previous lower bound.

A new investigation into dark energy, referred to as Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE), has shown that this model can effectively reproduce the evolution of the universe's equation of state parameter, w, across different epochs. To further enhance this theory's accuracy, a quintessence-based scenario with a new potential function, derived from the Tsallis form of the FRW metric, is proposed. This modified potential includes a harmonic term as well as a complex pole term with specified constraints. Analytical solutions for the quintessence field have been found, and a subsequent phase-space analysis was conducted to determine the suitable parameters for this theory. As part of the analysis, a numerical calculation was performed to visualize the phase-plane behavior. This theoretical framework's validity is confirmed by comparing its predicted values of the equation of state parameter, w, with their corresponding observed values.

Our study began with a small subset of the LAMOST's $K$2 photometric survey data to establish a prototype observatory that tracks changes in stars over time. To achieve this, we used our LSE time-domain exploration tool to process multiple epochs of data and identified interesting targets. Our results revealed 320 variable stars, consisting of 270 periodic and 50 unusual cases, as well as 1,863 stable stars with consistent brightness. These findings are comprised of 1 DD, 1 DR, 1 HD, 1 RB, 1 TCE, and 205 EAS, characterized by an unknown pattern of variation. To compare our approach with other programs, we also made a list of 1,863 stable stars and 270 periodic stars that were found during this pilot project. To facilitate further research, we created a publicly accessible database that contains our research observations, our findings regarding the behavior of these stellar objects, and relevant data from other sources as well. This means that 6,472 objects, consisting of 5,668 variable stars and 1,804 stable stars, along with other cases, are now available via a search engine that allows users to look up objects based on their characteristics in the LAMOST database.

True randomness is crucial in numerous fields such as cryptography and biology, yet high quality random numbers are difficult to generate. By utilizing the fragile nature of SRAM cells, which are sensitive to power fluctuations, it is possible to create high quality random numbers. Our previous research developed a method called SRAMP, which used supply voltage underscaling to generate random numbers from SRAM cells, but discovered that SRAMP was susceptible to a limited number of bits due to noise limitations. To address this issue, we developed TuRaN, which uses a advanced algorithm to increase the number of bits and improve the quality of random numbers. TuRaN achieves 80-90 entropies per bit with 1 MSI technology, producing 40-45 kbps true random bits. Additionally, TuRaN incurs minimal area overhead, requiring no existing firmware or hardware adjustments.

A new class of molecular devices has been developed that can process and store electronic information at the level of a single electron. The flexibility of these devices can be modified to exhibit a variety of behaviors by utilizing different materials and designs. To date, it has been challenging to build a full-scale electronic circuit using these devices because of their limited stability when subjected to electrical current. In this work, a design concept is presented that addresses this issue through the integration of a molecular memory element and an insulating component to divert excess charge. By doing so, it is possible to maintain the health of the memory element and ensure that it remains reliable over time. Computational models have been utilized to investigate the properties of the designed devices and explain their operating mechanisms. The results of these simulations have confirmed the effectiveness of this concept and paved the way for the creation of innovative single-electron technologies.

We develop a novel numerical approach for computing multi-loop Feynman integrals through general, causal representations. This method, using a lattice of discrete time points, evaluates the integral's leading and sub-leading components separately. Its finite parts can be determined from a lattice scalar product with a corresponding operator, while the transversality sector is analyzed using a causal Lippmann-Schwinger equation. Our approach is exemplified by obtaining all-order results for planar and non-planar double boxes, further validated by matching with known results at two and three loops. This method holds great potential for obtaining fully-causal representations of Feynman integrals, crucial for further applications in quantum field theory.

One-dimensional two-level quantum walks can be represented by a continuous time evolution operator, which has a unique periodic property. This discovery leads to a novel eigenstate expansion formula derived from the periodic structure of the evolution operator, facilitating the determination of eigenstates and eigenvalues through a straightforward computation method. Furthermore, this formulation enables the calculation of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in a one-dimensional two-level quantum walk by resolving a previously challenging integral in the literature.

This study examines the structural and thermodynamic characteristics of composite stars composed of quarks, encompassing both massive and lightweight objects, set against their respective ground states. To achieve this, the researcher combined the Sigma-omega-rho model with the MIT and NJL models, incorporating the Bogoliubov-Bose and Fermi approximation to describe the degenerate matter within these stars. To validate their findings, the researcher developed a theoretical framework to evaluate the mass and radius of these composite stars, thereby establishing model reliability. To further illustrate the feasibility of this model, the researcher highlighted the similarities between the properties of composite stars and those of ordinary stars, namely those consisting of nucleons. To round off, the researcher explored the effects of spin and Isospin degrees of freedom on the structure of these composite stars.

We investigate the optical system's non-degenerate ground state for its optomechanical interaction, utilizing the $q$-deformation method. This approach enables the transformation of the ground state into a mixed-state component, which facilitates the explanation of the system's behavior during switching processes. By analyzing the system's transmission and reflection patterns, we identify the relationships between these characteristics and the value of the deformation parameter $q$. Furthermore, the effects of the deformation on the system are observed to influence the transformation of optical waves between the two cavities and the formation of self-similar optical waves.

In a model where the Dual-Rotors Model's time- evolution operator includes an R-parity operator, the Hamiltonian's matrix representation exhibits a unique structure. This structure can be decomposed into two separate rotational components using the Casimir operators of the group $SO(1,1)$, leading to a set of exact solutions for the R-parity-scissors modes. Utilizing this decomposition, the exact closed-form solutions for the R-parity-scissors modes are derived in the Degenerate R-parity Scissors Model, and the exact deformed R-parity-scissors modes are derived in the Dual-Rotors Model's Degenerate R-parity Scissors subspaces. Additionally, the exact deformed R-parity-scissors modes are generalized to the non-Degenerate R-parity Scissors subspaces of the Dual-Rotor Model, and the exact deformed R-parity-scissors modes are further generalized to the non-Degenerate R-parity Scissors subspaces of the $SO(1,1)$-invariant Dual-Rotor Model.

In this study, we examine the rotational and orbital phenomena in ultrathin SiO films grown on Si substrates, focusing on the temporal evolution of these structures and their interrelation-ship. Additionally, we investigate how rotational variations affect the structural properties and investigate the structural differences between different loop patterns. Moreover, we make connections between the structural properties and variations in oxidation temperature, and provide a comprehensive explanation for the unique features of rotational and orbital variations in ultrathin SiO films on Si substrates.

We've discovered unique statistical characteristics of laser-cooled atoms within dissipative optical lattices, and our findings reveal considerable deviations from traditional thermal behavior. A combination of analytical and numerical methods shows that this phenomenon originates from the interplay between cooling and emission processes influenced by the optical structure. As a result, we observe considerable shifts in entropy, specific heat, and correlations, and these effects are controllable through variations in the dissipative rate and laser intensity. Of particular interest, we've found that for a certain laser pattern, the system can exhibit enhanced correlations beyond what's possible in a standard optical lattice.

This study offers insights into the higher-order connections among major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Litecoin, as well as their relationships with global shares and commodity indices. By applying a bivariate GARCH model, the research reveals significant correlations between cryptocurrencies and then explores their trading links with commodities and stock markets. The analysis demonstrates that cryptocurrency relationships with both markets and each other are characterized by complex, multi-way effects. In particular, the study discovers triadic connections among Ethereum, Litecoin, and commodity indices, as well as bilateral links between Bitcoin and global shares. These findings provide valuable insights for both academics and professionals in the cryptocurrency market.

The vibrational motion of tiny molecular clusters is not negligible and must be considered when modeling their structures to get an accurate representation. This is especially important in atmospheric clusters composed of acid and water, as their vibrational energy has a significant impact on their stability. By utilizing the path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) method at the density functional theory (DFT) level of calculation, the thermal and zero-point corrections of clusters composed of sulphuric acid and water have been determined. This treatment reveals that the vibrational motion significantly affects the energy distribution but has a lesser effect on the potential energy surface, leading to distinct classical and quantum mechanical behaviors in terms of tackiness and stability.

We establish the definitions for metrizable compactifications of pairs $(X, D)$ and analyze their topological characteristics, particularly their homeomorphism types. Furthermore, it's proven that if $(X, D)$ is compactly exactly recognizable, then its compactification $(X, D)$ possesses certain properties equivalent to being compactly recognizable. Additionally, a comprehensive study on the compactifications of functions from a group $(G, \cdot)$ to a metric space $(X, D)$ that are non-expansive and invariant under $G$ is presented, including the construction of their maximal compactifications. It's shown that for any given non-expansive function $f: G \to X$, its closure $(\bar{f}, \bar{D})$ is compactly exactly recognizable, and it possesses a unique maximal compactification $(\mathscr{X}_f, \mathscr{D}_f)$ that arises from extending $\bar{f}$ to a compact subset of $\mathscr{X}_f$. Moreover, it's demonstrated that the topological spaces of the compactifications $(\mathscr{X}_f, \mathscr{D}_f)$ are uniformly homeomorphic to compact subsets of $X$ when the metric space $(X, D)$ is compact.

The connection between thermal and electric responses in systems without charge density fluctuations can be described by Einstein's relations, which fails in certain cases with unusual boundary interactions as demonstrated by exceptional quantum anomalies. We observe that Einstein's relations also breaks down in certain chiral superfluids under specific boundary conditions, which can be compared to anomalies in liquid $^3$He. Our study involves theoretical calculations of thermal Hall conductivity in a spin-orbit coupled two-bands system with different types of boundary interactions, which fails to satisfy Einstein's relations. Additionally, our findings reveal that the thermal Hall conductivity can take on a finite value at the band gap when the SO coupling is weak, which can potentially serve as a candidate for a topological superfluid as a possible model of $^3$He-A, which also exhibits this property.

In various machine learning tasks, the inherent regularizing effects of network architecture have been found to contribute significantly to its performance. Through the integration of information-theoretic and statistical mechanics approaches, we aim to uncover the permanent regularizing impact of deep neural network architecture. Our findings indicate that the multiple stages within a neural network act as numerous regularizing factors, stemming from the considerable geometric complexity of its parameter space. Furthermore, we have developed a practical method for estimating the upper limit on the effective complexity, which can be employed to predict the optimal network size for a given problem. Interestingly, this regularizing impact may also manifest as an over-exploitation of feature interactions at the initial stages of the network.

A new approach for estimating the Wilson coefficient $C_{7}( \mu)$ in rare $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within the large operator effective field theory framework. This method provides a direct relationship between Wilson coefficients and experimentally measurable parameters at the level of tree-level diagrams. As a result, the Wilson coefficient $C_7(\mu)$ can be determined from data more quickly and with greater precision than with conventional methods that rely on resummation techniques or numerical simulations. We compare this new approach with other Wilson coefficient estimation methods and find that it can reduce uncertainty in $C_7(\mu)$ by up to 30% when combining it with existing analysis techniques. Although designed for $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, this new approach can also be applied to other $B\to V\mu^+\mu^-$ decays to estimate the Wilson coefficient $C_9(\mu)$.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  A notable approach involves supplementing limited training data with artificially created examples to address issues like diverse student writing.  We examine a more modest solution that employs pre-trained Language Models to process various types of student essays during prediction.  To support this method, we display a range of examples to the model, covering normal student submissions and then the test essay being evaluated.  We incorporate significant amounts of data to train the model and demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach with notable results.

The use of copulae-based models to analyze joint probability distributions has gained significant academic attention in recent years due to their versatility and numerous applications, including the modeling of financial risks and non-synthetic dependencies. In contrast, there is relatively limited research available on marginal dependence models that incorporate explicit notions of dependence between continuous random variables, largely due to the absence of a universally applicable measure of dependence for individual variables. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of existing research on copulae-based models, before delving into the advantages of marginal dependence models and introducing a novel measure of dependence called the mutual information, along with a non-parametric estimation method. The resulting mutual information model is found to surpass the accuracy of traditional copula-based methods in various applications, according to numerical testing and real-world data analysis. The associated software code is available at https://github.com/D-Salvador/MID/tree/master/MID.

A persistent social phenomenon observed across the globe is the tendency of higher social status to be passed down to subsequent generations. This phenomenon can be explained by the presence of opportunities that provide advantages in the pursuit of further opportunities. A model has been developed that captures the spirit of opportunity advancement through a set of trees, where each node represents a family unit and the edges signify inheritance of parental connections. In this context, the distribution of nodes in the trees follows a non-random pattern, with the majority concentrated at lower nodes and fewer at upper nodes, creating a disadvantaged upper class. When the trees evolve over time, the rate of node concentration at lower nodes increases, resulting in a higher rate of new nodes inheriting lower status. This model incorporates the concept of strategic decision-making, where family units compete to secure direct connections to higher status nodes, giving preferences to safer options that prioritize family well-being over the risk of gaining valuable connections to higher status nodes. However, families that choose the safer option may miss the chance to ascend socially, resulting in the creation of an upper class comprised of individuals from lower status backgrounds who managed to secure connections to higher status nodes.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, its association with a more secure DPoS consensus mechanism enables the preservation of notable properties such as transactional efficiency and minimal computational complexity.

We introduce a concept called space toughness for a linear system $Ax=b$, where $A$ is an $M\times N$ matrix, as a measure of its solability in relation to perturbations of $b$ and the condition number of $A$. A solation path, defined as the set of solutions for a series of perturbations in $b$, is used to gauge this solability. Given a linear system and a bound on system data, we seek to maximize the length of its solation paths. This objective mirrors approaches in linear space toughness that aim to maximize the length of solation paths while varying the right-hand side of a linear system within a bound on system data. To quantify our objective, we define the general linear space toughness of $A$ as the infimum of bounds on the length of solation paths for a given system and the condition number of $A$. Similarly, we can define specific linear space toughness by considering specific forms for $A$, such as when it is comprised of diagonal or triangular entries. We show that for an $M\times N$ matrix $A$, its general linear space toughness is greater than or equal to $\sqrt{\frac{M}{N}}\cdot\kappa(A)$ and its specific linear space toughness for diagonal and triangular matrices follows a similar lower bound in relation to the size and condition number of the matrix.
